evidence.quote: Jiyuan Hu, PhD Associate Professor, Department of Population Health

research.text: As an associate professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine’s Department of Population Health, Division of Biostatistics, my primary research interests lie in the development of statistical, computational, and machine learning approaches for the analysis of high-dimensional ‘-omics’ data, EHR data, and other multi-modal data. I collaborate on broad biomedical research projects throughout the school and provide biostatistical support for randomized/cluster-randomized/pragmatic clinical trials.

name: PhD Ting-Fang Lee
title_on_roster: Research Assistant Professor, Department of Population Health

position.value: Research Assistant Professor, Department of Population Health

evidence.quote: Ting-Fang Lee, PhD Research Assistant Professor, Department of Population Health

research.text: My research focus primarily encompasses two areas of study. Firstly, I am dedicated to develop innovative methods and statistical methodologies tailored for the analysis of intricate data structures characterized by complex dependencies. These include but are not limited to scenarios involving repeated measurements over time, correlations between interrelated variables such as those observed between eyes in medical studies, and network-based studies. Secondly, I am interested to the application of advanced mathematical tools to machine learning algorithms. Specifically, I aim to exploit these tools to conceptualize and quantitatively measure health disparities arising from electronic medical records.

name: PhD Yidan Shi
title_on_roster: Assistant Professor, Department of Population Health

position.value: Assistant Professor, Department of Population Health

evidence.quote: Yidan Shi, PhD Assistant Professor, Department of Population Health

research.text: My research focuses on developing and applying advanced statistical methodologies in survival analysis, longitudinal data analysis, and causal inference, with an emphasis on addressing complex sampling conditions, mismeasured outcomes, and disease heterogeneity. I integrate event history data with multi-omics data and machine learning models to enhance predictive accuracy and generate deeper insights. Much of my collaborative work explores disease progression, risk factors, and treatment effects across aging, neurology, cancer, and mental health, with a particular focus on Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). My collaborative research also include clinical trials on interventions for opioid use and longitudinal follow-up studies for survivors on the 9/11 World Trade Center (WTC) attacks.

research.text: My primary research interests focus on developing statistical methodologies for high-throughput data, including sequencing data (genomics, transcriptomics, metagenomics, microbiome) as well as proteomics and metabolomics, with a focus on integrating these omics datasets. I am also involved in a wide range of biomedical projects, including clinical trials, study design, personalized nutrition, health disparities, health interventions, basic science, xenotransplantation, and epidemiological studies. As PI of a pilot study supported by the NYU Center for the Study of Asian American Health (CSAAH, NIH-NIMHD U54MD000538-19), I developed a novel microbial causal mediation analytic tool to explore the role of the microbiome in health disparities.

My expertise spans clinical trial design across all phases, Bayesian modeling, causal inference, and the analysis of large observational and real-world healthcare data, including electronic health records and population-based registries. I work closely with multidisciplinary clinical teams, with a particular focus on oncology, radiation oncology, neurology, orthopedics, and other data-intensive clinical domains. research.text: I am an Assistant Professor of biostatistics within the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, where I conduct research in the design, conduct, and analysis of clinical trials. My work primarily develops and tests interventions that utilize behavioral economic theory and digital health tools to improve clinical outcomes for chronic conditions, including diabetes and dementia. I am also interested in pragmatic studies embedded within electronic health records, and methods for extracting evidence from real world data in the context of Expanded Access programs.

research.text: My research focuses on the development of non-parametric statistical methods for causal inference from observational and randomized studies with complex datasets, using machine learning. This includes but is not limited to mediation analysis, methods for continuous exposures, longitudinal data including survival analysis, and efficiency guarantees with covariate adjustment in randomized trials. I am also interested in general semi-parametric theory, machine learning, and high-dimensional data.

research.text: I am an Assistant Professor in the Division of Biostatistics within the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. My research centers on the development and application of statistical methods for causal inference, with a particular emphasis on comparative effectiveness and health policy evaluation. Currently, I am developing estimators for quasi-experimental designs to assess treatment effects using observational data involving real-world challenges such as continuous exposures, interference, and clustered or longitudinal data structures. My work frequently draws on semiparametric estimation theory to construct robust estimators that integrate flexible modeling approaches like machine learning into causal inference frameworks. evidence.quote: Nicholas Illenberger, PhD Assistant Professor, Department of Population Health

research.text: I am an assistant professor in the Department of Population Health’s Division of Biostatistics. My research combines insights from the areas of causal inference, semiparametric estimation, and cost-effectiveness analyses to address important issues in health services research. In particular, my methodological work develops approaches for assessing treatment effect heterogeneity using observational data from complex longitudinal and clustered data settings. This work is critical in determining which populations may most benefit from additional interventions in low-resource settings.

research.text: I am interested in developing novel methodologies for solving biostatistical problems with real-world applications. My two primary research areas include semiparametric and nonparametric methods in survival analysis, specifically truncation and interval censoring of survival times, and measurement error problems for high-dimensional data. My research often has a computational aspect including parallel computing using high performance computing facilities. I have written novel R codes and Fortran subroutines for my research which can be found on my GitHub page below or on the CRAN-R Project website.
